questions.question: What does API stand for?

explanation.correct: API stands for Application Programming Interface — a set of rules allowing two software systems to communicate.
explanation.why: Option A confuses Protocol with Programming. Options C and D are not real AWS/IT terms.

questions.question: What is the primary role of AWS API Gateway?

options.text: Act as a front door between clients and backend services
Monitor CPU usage of EC2 instances

explanation.correct: API Gateway acts as a fully managed front door — receiving client requests, validating them, and routing them to the correct backend service.
explanation.why: A is S3/DynamoDB. B is S3 Static Hosting. D is CloudWatch. API Gateway is the request router/gateway.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is used to CREATE a new resource?

explanation.correct: POST is used to create new resources — like creating a new user account or placing a new order.
explanation.why: GET reads data, DELETE removes it, PUT updates/replaces existing data. POST = Create in CRUD.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is used to READ or retrieve data?

explanation.correct: GET retrieves data from the server without modifying it. It is the Read operation in CRUD.
explanation.why: POST creates, PUT updates/replaces, PATCH partially updates. GET is always read-only.

questions.question: What does a 404 HTTP status code mean?

options.text: Resource or path was not found

explanation.correct: 404 Not Found means the requested URL path does not exist or has not been defined in the API Gateway.
explanation.why: 500 = server crashed, 401 = not authenticated, 200 = success. 404 is a client-side error — wrong path.

questions.question: What does a 200 HTTP status code indicate?

explanation.correct: 200 OK means the request was processed successfully. It is the standard success response.
explanation.why: 201 = created, 403 = forbidden, 5xx = server errors. 200 is the baseline success code.

questions.question: What are the four basic parts of an HTTP request?

explanation.correct: Every HTTP request contains a Method (what action), URL (where), Headers (extra info like auth tokens), and Body (data payload for POST/PUT/PATCH).
explanation.why: Options A, C, D mix up different concepts. The four structural parts of an HTTP request are Method, URL, Headers, and Body.

questions.question: What is the difference between 401 and 403 status codes?

options.text: 401 = not authenticated, 403 = authenticated but not authorized
Both mean the same thing — access denied

explanation.correct: 401 Unauthorized means the user has not proven who they are (not logged in). 403 Forbidden means the user is identified but does not have permission.
explanation.why: They are often confused. 401 = Who are you? 403 = I know who you are, but you cannot enter.

questions.question: Which two AWS services are supported by Gateway VPC Endpoints?

explanation.correct: Gateway VPC Endpoints only support Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB. All other services require Interface Endpoints.
explanation.why: SNS, SQS, CloudWatch, Lambda, RDS — all require Interface Endpoints. Only S3 and DynamoDB have free Gateway Endpoints.

questions.question: What does a VPC Endpoint eliminate?

options.text: The need for an EC2 instance
The need for internet access to reach AWS services

explanation.correct: VPC Endpoints allow private resources in a VPC to communicate with AWS services without going through the public internet, NAT Gateway, or VPN.
explanation.why: EC2, IAM, and VPC are still needed. What VPC Endpoints eliminate is the requirement for internet access to reach AWS services.

questions.question: What HTTP status code range indicates a client-side error?

explanation.correct: 4xx status codes indicate client-side errors — the request itself was malformed, unauthorized, forbidden, or requested a non-existent resource.
explanation.why: 1xx = informational, 2xx = success, 5xx = server-side errors. 4xx always means the problem is with the incoming request.

questions.question: Which part of the HTTP request body is included in?

options.text: Only POST, PUT, and PATCH requests

explanation.correct: The body is present only when sending data to the server — POST (create), PUT (update/replace), and PATCH (partial update). GET and DELETE typically do not have a body.
explanation.why: GET retrieves data — there is nothing to send. DELETE identifies what to remove via URL, not body. Only write operations carry a body.

questions.question: A company wants to build a microservices app with separate services for orders, payments, and shipping. How should they expose this to clients using API Gateway?

options.text: Create three separate API Gateways, one per service
Create one API Gateway with three resources (/orders, /payments, /shipping) routing to each backend
Skip API Gateway and expose each EC2's IP address directly
Use one Lambda function to handle all three services

explanation.correct: One API Gateway with multiple resources (paths) is the correct pattern. It provides a single entry point while routing internally to each independent microservice backend.
explanation.why: Multiple gateways create management overhead and force clients to know multiple URLs. Exposing EC2 IPs is insecure. One Lambda for all = not microservices.

questions.question: What is a 'stage' in API Gateway?

options.text: A type of Lambda function trigger
A named reference to a deployment of your API (e.g., dev, prod)
A geographic region for the API
A security policy attached to the API

explanation.correct: A stage is a named snapshot of your API deployment. Common stages are dev, staging, and prod — allowing you to test changes safely before affecting production.
explanation.why: Stages are not related to Lambda triggers, regions, or security policies. They are deployment environments within the same API.

questions.question: Which API Gateway type is recommended for most use cases due to lower cost and latency?

explanation.correct: HTTP API is up to 71% cheaper than REST API and has lower latency — recommended for most proxy integrations to Lambda or HTTP backends.
explanation.why: REST API is feature-rich but costlier. WebSocket is for real-time apps. SOAP API is not an AWS API Gateway type.

questions.question: An EC2 in a private subnet needs to call CloudWatch APIs privately. Which VPC Endpoint type is required?

explanation.correct: Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) support CloudWatch and virtually all AWS services. Gateway Endpoints only support S3 and DynamoDB.
explanation.why: NAT Gateway and Internet Gateway both send traffic over the public internet. Gateway Endpoint does not support CloudWatch.

questions.question: What is the key difference between how Gateway and Interface VPC Endpoints route traffic?

options.text: Gateway uses route table entries; Interface creates an ENI with a private IP
Gateway creates an ENI; Interface uses route tables
Both create ENIs in the subnet

explanation.correct: Gateway Endpoints add an entry to the route table to redirect S3/DynamoDB traffic through the AWS network. Interface Endpoints create an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) with a private IP inside your subnet.
explanation.why: Understanding the mechanism difference is critical for exam questions about subnet design and cost.

questions.question: What does API Gateway throttling protect against?

options.text: Backend services being overwhelmed by too many requests

explanation.correct: Throttling limits the number of requests per second allowed through API Gateway, protecting backend services from being overwhelmed by traffic spikes or DDoS attacks.
explanation.why: Authentication handles unauthorized access. Data integrity is handled by TLS. Method validation is part of request validation, not throttling.

questions.question: What is the default request per second limit for AWS API Gateway?

explanation.correct: API Gateway has a default throttling limit of 10,000 requests per second with a burst limit of 5,000 requests. Both can be increased by requesting a service quota increase.
explanation.why: The 5,000 figure is the burst limit, not the sustained RPS limit. 10,000 RPS is the account-level default.

questions.question: A developer gets a 500 error from their API. Where should they look first?

options.text: Check if the URL path is correct
Check the backend — Lambda code or EC2 application logs
Verify the HTTP method is correct

explanation.correct: 500 Internal Server Error means the backend crashed or threw an unhandled exception. The client's request was fine — the problem is server-side, so check Lambda logs or EC2 application logs in CloudWatch.
explanation.why: Wrong URL = 404, wrong method = 405, auth issue = 401/403. 500 always points to a backend failure.

questions.question: Which authorization mechanism in API Gateway allows a custom Lambda function to validate tokens and return IAM policies?

explanation.correct: A Lambda Authorizer is a custom Lambda function that receives the incoming token, validates it, and returns an IAM policy allowing or denying access to the API.
explanation.why: IAM Auth uses AWS signatures for internal calls. Cognito handles user pools. Lambda Authorizer is the flexible custom option for any token type (JWT, OAuth, custom).

questions.question: A team builds an app where users can collaboratively edit a document in real time — changes from one user instantly appear for all others. Which API Gateway type is most appropriate?

explanation.correct: WebSocket API maintains a persistent bidirectional connection — the server can push updates to all connected clients instantly without clients needing to poll.
explanation.why: REST and HTTP APIs are request-response — the client must ask for updates. Gateway Endpoint is not an API type, it's a VPC networking concept.

questions.question: A company needs to connect 10 different EC2 services in their VPC to 10 different external SaaS partners' services privately. Which AWS feature enables this at scale?

explanation.correct: AWS PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints) allows private connectivity to services across VPCs and AWS accounts without exposing traffic to the public internet — ideal for SaaS integrations at scale.
explanation.why: VPC Peering links entire VPCs (not scalable for many partners). NAT uses public internet. VPN adds unnecessary complexity for AWS-to-AWS service connections.

questions.question: You have a REST API in API Gateway with caching enabled at TTL=300 seconds. A backend update changes user data. What happens to cached responses?

options.text: Cache is automatically invalidated when backend data changes
Clients receive stale cached responses until TTL expires unless cache is manually invalidated
Cache is disabled automatically during data updates
API Gateway re-fetches data every 60 seconds regardless of TTL

explanation.correct: API Gateway caching is time-based. The cache does not automatically detect backend data changes. Clients will receive stale responses until TTL expires (300s) unless you manually flush the cache via the console or API.
explanation.why: AWS does not automatically watch for backend data changes to invalidate cache. This is a key architectural consideration — caching is best for rarely-changing data.

questions.question: Which combination correctly identifies a single unique API operation in API Gateway?

explanation.correct: A unique API operation is always the combination of a resource path (/users, /orders) AND an HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE). The same path with different methods is a different operation.
explanation.why: Path alone allows multiple operations (GET /users and POST /users are different). Method alone doesn't tell you what resource. Stage is a deployment concept, not an operation identifier.

questions.question: An EC2 in a private subnet uses a Gateway VPC Endpoint for S3. The endpoint is created but the EC2 still cannot reach S3. What is most likely misconfigured?

options.text: The EC2 security group is blocking HTTPS
The route table associated with the private subnet does not include the endpoint route
The S3 bucket does not allow VPC traffic
Gateway Endpoints cannot be used in private subnets

explanation.correct: Gateway Endpoints work by modifying the route table. If the private subnet's route table was not selected during endpoint creation, traffic still routes through the NAT Gateway or internet — bypassing the endpoint entirely.
explanation.why: Security groups don't apply to S3 (bucket policies do). S3 bucket policies default to allow from the account. Gateway Endpoints work in private subnets — that's their primary use case.

questions.question: Which status code would a client receive if they send a request to /orders but the API Gateway only has /order defined?

explanation.correct: 404 Not Found — /orders is not a defined resource in API Gateway. The path does not exist in the API configuration, so the gateway cannot route the request.
explanation.why: 401/403 relate to auth, not wrong paths. 500 is a backend error. The client specified a path that API Gateway doesn't recognize — classic 404.

questions.question: A company wants to use Interface VPC Endpoints to privately access multiple AWS services. What is created in each Availability Zone where the endpoint is configured?

options.text: An Elastic Network Interface (ENI) with a private IP address

explanation.correct: Interface Endpoints create an Elastic Network Interface (ENI) in the specified subnet within each AZ. This ENI gets a private IP from the subnet's range and serves as the entry point for PrivateLink traffic.
explanation.why: NAT Gateways are public-internet-facing. Interface Endpoints don't create subnets or route table entries — that's Gateway Endpoints. ENIs are the core mechanism of PrivateLink.

questions.question: An API is publicly accessible and receives millions of requests. One user sends 100,000 requests/minute trying to scrape data. Which API Gateway feature AND configuration would best address this?

options.text: Enable caching — cache responses to reduce backend load
Enable throttling with per-client usage plans and API keys
Switch from REST API to HTTP API
Move the backend to a larger EC2 instance

explanation.correct: Usage plans + API keys in REST API allow you to set per-client rate limits. A client exceeding their limit receives 429 Too Many Requests, protecting the backend from abuse while allowing legitimate clients normal access.
explanation.why: Caching reduces backend calls but doesn't stop the abusive client from sending requests. HTTP API doesn't add per-client limits. Larger EC2 doesn't solve the bad actor problem.

questions.question: A startup wants to expose their backend Lambda functions via API Gateway for a mobile app. They need low cost, low latency, and support for JWT authentication via Cognito. Which API type fits?

options.text: REST API — for full feature set
HTTP API — lower cost with native Cognito JWT auth support
WebSocket API — for mobile push notifications
SOAP API — for enterprise mobile integration

explanation.correct: HTTP API natively supports JWT authorization (including Cognito), is significantly cheaper than REST API, has lower latency, and integrates well with Lambda. It is ideal for mobile backend APIs that don't require REST API-only features like caching or request transformation.
explanation.why: REST API adds unnecessary cost for this use case. WebSocket is for real-time bidirectional apps. SOAP API is not an AWS API Gateway type.
